Standard
STAN-derd
n.
From Old French estendard, a banner, related to extendere, to spread out. Webster 1828: an ensign of war; a flag; also, a rule or measure of authority. In the Authorized Version the word is military and tribal — the four great banners under which Israel camped and marched — and once prophetic, of the standard the Spirit lifts against a flood.

Biblical Definition

A standard in Scripture is the banner that tells a man where he belongs. Israel in the wilderness did not camp at random: Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch (Numbers 2:2). Four standards ordered the whole camp — Judah on the east, Reuben on the south, Ephraim on the west, Dan on the north (Numbers 2:10, 18, 25) — and the same order governed the march: In the first place went the standard of the camp of the children of Judah (Numbers 10:14). Two features are doctrinal. The standards face inward: every tribe pitches by its banner, but all of them pitch about the tabernacle. Identity within the covenant people is real and ordered, and it is organized around the presence of God rather than against the other tribes. And the standard governs both rest and movement; a man knew where to sleep and when to march by the same flag. The prophetic use lifts the figure to God Himself: When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him (Isaiah 59:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives STANDARD as an ensign of war; the flag of a troop or company; and, in a second sense, that which is established by authority as a rule or measure — a standard of weight, of value, of faith. Both senses are alive in English; the KJV uses the first.

expand to see more

STANDARD, n. — An ensign of war; a staff with a flag or colors; the ensign of a regiment or troop.

That which is established by sovereign power as a rule or measure; as, a standard of weights and measures; a standard of value.

Hence, a test or criterion by which anything is tried — a standard of faith, a standard of morals.

The KJV’s use is uniformly the banner. But the second sense is not foreign to the theology: a people gathered under one ensign around one tabernacle is a people governed by one rule.

Key Scripture

Numbers 1:52 — "And the children of Israel shall pitch their tents, every man by his own camp, and every man by his own standard, throughout their hosts."

Numbers 2:2 — "Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch."

Numbers 2:10 — "On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben according to their armies: and the captain of the children of Reuben shall be Elizur the son of Shedeur."

Numbers 10:14 — "In the first place went the standard of the camp of the children of Judah according to their armies: and over his host was Nahshon the son of Amminadab."

Isaiah 59:19 — "So shall they fear the name of the LORD from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun. When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him."

Modern Corruption

The word is corrupted when the banner is detached from the tabernacle — when tribal identity becomes an end in itself and the camp is organized around what distinguishes the tribes rather than around the God at the centre.

expand to see more

Numbers 2:2 gives both halves of the order and the modern age keeps only one. Every man pitches by his own standard — identity is real, particular, and inherited, and Scripture does not dissolve it. But every standard pitches about the tabernacle of the congregation, and that is the half now routinely dropped. Where the church is arranged into caucuses whose banners face outward, and where the question “which group are you” governs more than the question “whose presence are we gathered around,” the camp of Numbers 2 has been rebuilt without its centre. Paul settles the ordering in 1 Corinthians 1:12-13: every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos… Is Christ divided?

The second corruption is the flattening of the standard into a preference. Isaiah 59:19 has the Spirit of the LORD lifting a standard against an invading flood; that is a war banner, planted where a line will be held. A church that has no standard has not become welcoming; it has become undefended. The confessions serve exactly this function — the 1689 is a banner raised so that a congregation knows what it is gathered around and where the line runs when the flood comes in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two Hebrew words lie behind the English. Degel is the tribal standard of Numbers; nes is the raised signal or pole, the word behind Isaiah’s standard and behind the name Jehovah-nissi.

expand to see more

Hebrew degel (H1714) — a banner or standard; the four tribal ensigns of the wilderness camp (Numbers 1:52; 2:2, 10; 10:14).

Hebrew 'oth (H226) — a sign or ensign; paired with degel in Numbers 2:2 as the ensign of their father's house.

Hebrew nes (H5251) — a pole, signal, or raised standard (Isaiah 59:19; Isaiah 11:10, the root lifted for an ensign of the people).

Hebrew Yahweh-nissi (Exodus 17:15) — the LORD my banner, the altar Moses built after Amalek; the same nes.

The Song of Solomon uses degel of love itself: his banner over me was love (Song of Solomon 2:4).

Usage

"Every man by his own standard (Numbers 1:52) — order in the camp, not uniformity; each tribe knows its place."

"Far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch (Numbers 2:2) — the banners face a centre."

"The Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him (Isaiah 59:19) — the war banner God plants when the enemy comes in like a flood."
